characters: Efua: a girl of thirteen, JHS uniform, practical and thoughtful.
Nana Ama: her grandmother, patient and wise.
Kwabena: her classmate, confident and always looking for shortcuts.
Auntie Dede: a market trader who gives Efua advice.

narrationPlan.voice: Natural, mature storyteller, Ghanaian English. Subtle character differences, no caricature.
notes: Numbers must be spoken clearly and consistently with the text (check twelve, eight, forty, twenty, twenty-five, eleven, nine, thirteen).
Names go through the pronunciation dictionary; all entries are still awaiting native-speaker review.

music: No background music: text-first reading experience for older learners. Optional soft ambience toggle only.
culturalNotes: Groundnut cakes (nkate cake and similar sweets) are a familiar local treat; a reviewer should confirm the recipe description and the realism of prices in cedis for the intended year.
The names are Akan day names (Efua, Kwabena, Ama); Dede’s origin must be confirmed.
reviewQuestions: Are the prices realistic for the intended region and year? (Amounts are illustrative.)
Does the dilemma suit JHS and avoid moralising?
Is the groundnut-cake recipe description (roasted groundnuts and sugar) right for what learners know as groundnut cakes?
Is the cost-per-pack arithmetic (65 pesewas, 13 cedis for twenty) consistent everywhere?

pages.brief: Nana Ama and Efua stir a pot of golden sugar and groundnuts together on a charcoal stove, steam rising in the morning light. Must show: the pot of glossy golden groundnuts; Nana’s wooden spoon; steam in the light. Camera: medium two-shot, slightly above the pot. Lighting: warm window light with golden steam.
pages.narration: Warm, unhurried, a smile in the voice. Let "quick hands and patient eyes" sound like a saying Nana Ama repeats.

image.alt: A thirteen-year-old girl stirs a pot beside her grandmother in a warm kitchen, golden groundnuts and sugar glowing in the pot.

pages.brief: Efua, hopeful, looks to her grandmother, who playfully points to an exercise book and pencil on the kitchen table. Must show: blue exercise book with pencil; finished groundnut cakes cooling on a tray. Camera: medium two-shot at table height. Lighting: soft late-morning window light.
pages.narration: Bright and hopeful for the plan; Nana Ama gentle and teasing.

pages.brief: Efua writes neat columns of costs and profit in her exercise book at a small table under a warm lamp. Must show: exercise book with simple handwritten sums (numbers only, no readable words); pencil in hand; lamp glow on her face. Camera: close medium shot over her shoulder showing the page. Lighting: single warm lamp, deep indigo background.
pages.narration: Measured, working-it-out pace; slow and clear on every number (twelve, one, eight, forty).

pages.brief: At the school gate, Efua hands a paper-wrapped pack to a smiling student; a cloth bag of leftover packs sits at her feet. Must show: paper-wrapped packs on a small table; a cloth bag of leftover packs at her feet; two or three students in uniform. Camera: medium shot, Efua at right, queue at left. Lighting: late-afternoon golden light.
pages.narration: Picks up pace for the sales, then slows and dips on "gone a little soft".

pages.brief: Kwabena leans in near the gate, glancing at the bag of soft cakes, while Efua looks uncertain. Must show: the bag of soft cakes; Kwabena’s persuasive grin; Efua’s uncertain look. Camera: medium two-shot, slightly low. Lighting: late-afternoon, shade under the tree.
pages.narration: Kwabena smooth, friendly, reasonable-sounding. Not a villain.

pages.brief: Kwabena smiles confidently and points at the old packs, as if it is the most sensible idea in the world; Efua hesitates. Must show: old packs in the bag; Kwabena’s confident gesture; Efua hesitating. Camera: two-shot, eye level, shallow depth of field. Lighting: soft shade with warm highlights.
pages.narration: Confident, easy. A beat of silence after "fresh today" before the final clause. Efua’s silence lands.

pages.brief: Alone by lamplight, Efua sits still with her exercise book open, thinking hard, a deep blue night sky in the window. Must show: open exercise book with numbers; lamp glow; night sky in the window. Camera: medium shot from the side, lamp as the key light. Lighting: warm lamp, indigo night, gentle moonlight.
pages.narration: Slow, reflective. Let each number breathe. Slow further on "trust" and lower the voice on the last line.

pages.brief: Auntie Dede arranges a pyramid of tomatoes at her stall and speaks kindly to Efua, who listens carefully. Must show: pyramid of tomatoes; Auntie Dede’s red-and-gold head-tie; Efua listening. Camera: medium two-shot with the tomato pyramid in the foreground. Lighting: warm morning light through the cloth awning.
pages.narration: Auntie Dede warm, firm, experienced; a gentle smile in the voice on "garden".

pages.brief: Efua’s hands fill a paper pack with extra groundnut cakes and write the date on a small label; a second bag is marked as half price. Must show: extra groundnuts in the pack; handwritten date on the label (numbers only); a separate bag marked for half price, shown with a simple symbol, no readable words. Camera: close-up on her hands and the packs, her face softly visible. Lighting: warm kitchen light.
pages.narration: Quiet pride, steady pace. Read the label text clearly.

pages.brief: A longer queue of cheerful students at the school gate; Efua serves with a smile. Must show: the long queue; Efua serving; the half-price bag on the table. Camera: wide medium shot, queue leading the eye to Efua. Lighting: golden afternoon.

Kwabena, at the front of the queue, sheepishly smiles as Efua holds out a fresh pack of groundnut cakes. Must show: Kwabena sheepish; the pack being held out; the queue behind him. Camera: medium two-shot, warm and friendly. Lighting: golden afternoon, soft rim light.
pages.narration: Kwabena a little sheepish, honest. Efua’s last line dry and warm: she charges him, and it is funny.

pages.brief: Efua writes the date at the top of a fresh page in her exercise book, smiling quietly, a jar of groundnuts beside her. Must show: fresh page; jar of groundnuts; quiet smile. Camera: medium close shot, warm and calm. Lighting: warm lamp, soft indigo night.
pages.narration: Satisfied, understated; slow down on the last sentence and let "honestly" settle.

teacherGuide.overview: Efua starts a small groundnut-cake business and is tempted by a classmate’s shortcuts. The story joins real arithmetic (cost, revenue, profit) to a choice about honesty, and shows that a trustworthy reputation is part of a business’s value.
learningGoals: Work out cost, income and profit from a simple business and check a claim against the numbers.
Explain why trust and honesty matter to customers and to a business over time.
Infer a character’s reasoning and the meaning of a metaphor ("customers are like a garden").
Apply the story to a real choice in the learner’s own life.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics
subjectLinks.link: Money, cost and profit; checking a claim with calculation.

beforeReading: Ask: "Have you ever bought something from a school-gate seller? What made you go back, or not?"
Pre-teach: profit, cost, trust. Write "profit = money in − money spent" on the board.
whileReading: After page 3, pause for the profit activity: check every learner can get to eight cedis.
After page 6, ask for predictions before reading on (the prediction activity).
After page 7, let learners check Kwabena’s "twice the profit" claim with Efua’s numbers.
afterReading: Put the events in order, then retell the story in three sentences.
Have learners recalculate with the final recipe: cost 65 pesewas per pack, selling at one cedi.
discussion: Was Kwabena a bad person, or someone giving poor advice? How do you know?
Efua made less profit on some days. What did she gain that the sums alone do not show?
How was selling leftover cakes at half price different from calling them fresh?
What does "Customers are like a garden" mean? Can you think of another comparison?
reflection: Think of a time you were tempted to take a shortcut. What did you do, and what would you do now?
What do people say about you when you are not there? How could you build a reputation you are proud of?
Where in your own life (school, home, a small job, a class project) does honesty cost you something in the short term and pay off later?
Who is your "Auntie Dede", someone whose advice you trust? What makes them trustworthy?

mathsExtension.task: Efua sells all 20 packs at 1 cedi each. Cost 12 cedis. What is the profit?
On Monday she sold 14 packs of the 20 she made. What was her profit?
mathsExtension.answer: 14 − 12 = 2 cedis (the six unsold packs were already paid for).

mathsExtension.task: With fewer groundnuts, 20 packs cost 9 cedis. What is the profit if all 20 sell? How much more than 8 cedis is that?
mathsExtension.answer: 20 − 9 = 11 cedis, which is 3 cedis more. Kwabena promised "twice", which would be 16.

mathsExtension.task: The honest recipe costs 65 pesewas a pack. What do 25 packs cost, and what is the profit if all sell at 1 cedi?
mathsExtension.answer: 25 × 65 = 1,625 pesewas = 16.25 cedis. Profit 25 − 16.25 = 8.75 cedis, more than the original 8 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Challenge: Efua sells 5 half-price packs (50 pesewas each) and 20 full-price packs a day. Cost: 16.25 cedis for 25 packs. What is the profit?
mathsExtension.answer: Income 20 + 2.50 = 22.50 cedis. Profit 22.50 − 16.25 = 6.25 cedis. Honest half-price selling costs a little, and still earns trust.

support: Use whole-cedi numbers only (pages 3 and 7) and a number line for subtraction.
Read pages aloud in "Listen" mode and discuss with a partner before answering.
stretch: Ask learners to design their own small business and cost it, including how they would handle leftovers honestly.
Compare Kwabena’s claim with Efua’s calculation and write a two-sentence rebuttal.

culturalNotes: The names are Akan day names: Efua (a girl born on Friday), Kwabena (a boy born on Tuesday), Ama (a girl born on Saturday). Dede is used in several Ghanaian communities; a reviewer should confirm its origin before it is described in print.
"Nana" is a respectful title for an elder or grandparent. "Auntie" is a common courtesy title for a woman who is not necessarily a relative.
Groundnut cakes (nkate cake and similar sweets) are a familiar snack. A local reviewer should confirm the recipe description.
localiseThis: Prices are illustrative: check that 12 cedis for 20 packs and a 1 cedi selling price suit your area and year, and adjust the numbers and answers together.
Choose a school uniform colour that matches your school if learners will see illustrations of the gate.

reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.

pronunciation.guidance: three soft syllables, "eh-FOO-ah". A two-syllable "EH-fwah" is also heard in English speech.
reviewerNotes: Choose between "eh-FOO-ah" (3 syllables) and "EH-fwah" (2) for the narrator voice.
Supply IPA and mark tone if wanted.
Confirm language of origin and meaning before it appears in teacher notes.
